title: Small vs Large Offices: How Volume Changes Upholstery and Partition Steam Cleaning Prices
seoTitle: Small vs Large Upholstery Partition Steam Cleaning: Volume Pricing
metaDescription: Small vs large upholstery partition steam cleaning: about $71–$108 per workstation in a 2,000 sq ft suite vs $49–$87 at 30,000 sq ft. Compare your quotes.
excerpt: Steam cleaning chairs and cubicle panels costs noticeably more per workstation in a small suite than on a large floor, because minimums, mobilization, and setup time are fixed. Here is how volume pricing works from 2,000 sq ft offices to 25,000+ sq ft buildings, and how small tenants can claw back some of the scale advantage.
quickAnswer: Per-unit prices for upholstery and fabric panel extraction fall as volume rises: a 2,000 sq ft suite with about 12 workstations typically pays $18–$30 per task chair and $0.90–$1.25 per sq ft of panel fabric, or roughly $71–$108 per workstation all-in. A 25,000+ sq ft floor with 140 workstations often pays $10–$20 per chair and $0.55–$0.90 per sq ft, or about $49–$87 per workstation. The gap comes from $90–$135 visit minimums, mobilization fees, and setup hours being spread over far more pieces.

blocks.text: Why unit prices fall as the job gets bigger

Every upholstery extraction job carries a fixed cost before the first chair is touched. The vendor loads a heated extractor, hoses, hand tools, pre-spray, and fans; drives to the site; checks in with security; finds a utility sink and dedicated outlet; tests fabric codes; and lays out floor protection. That fixed block typically consumes 45 to 90 minutes of specialty labor at $55–$95 per hour, or about $40–$140, before any production. On a 12-chair order it is a large share of the invoice; on a 180-chair order it nearly disappears.

Production also speeds up with volume. On a large floor, a two-person crew can run a station-to-station rhythm: one tech vacuums and pre-sprays while the other extracts, so each piece gets full dwell time without idle waiting. In a small suite, a single tech has to do every step serially. That workflow difference alone can move throughput from about 4 chairs per hour to 6 or 7.

blocks.title: Read the per-workstation line
blocks.text: The large floor pays roughly 20% to 30% less per workstation than the small suite for identical work. That spread mirrors how routine janitorial rates fall from $0.12–$0.20 per sq ft under 2,500 sq ft to $0.05–$0.10 per sq ft above 25,000 sq ft.
Where large buildings lose part of the advantage
Scale is not free. Large floors bring their own cost drivers that a careful buyer should expect to see on the quote, and that can erode the per-unit discount if they are not managed.

items: Multi-night scheduling: 140 workstations cannot dry overnight in one pass on a single circuit, so the job may span two to four nights, each with its own setup.
Electrical load: heated extractors draw significant current; tripped breakers on older floors cost crew time.
Furniture variety: mixed chair generations with different fabric codes slow production and may require solvent or low-moisture methods on S-coded pieces.
Security and freight elevators: badge escorts and elevator reservations in multi-tenant towers add waiting time.
Moisture management: more wet fabric at once means more air movers and HVAC coordination to hit a 2 to 6 hour dry time.

blocks.text: How small offices can capture volume pricing

A 2,000 sq ft suite will never match a 30,000 sq ft floor, but it can narrow the gap. The goal is to make the job bigger, simpler, or easier to schedule, so the vendor's fixed cost is spread across more billable work.

items.name: Combine with your regular janitorial visit
items.text: If your nightly vendor offers extraction, schedule it on a regular service night; the mobilization fee is often waived because the crew is already on site.

items.name: Bundle chairs, panels, and carpet spots
items.text: Adding reception seating and carpet spot extraction can push the order past the project minimum so every dollar buys production rather than setup.

items.name: Coordinate with neighboring tenants
items.text: Ask building management whether other suites want the same service the same week; vendors often discount stacked jobs in one building.

items.name: Pre-stage the space
items.text: Clear desks, push chairs to aisles, and identify a utility sink and outlet in advance so the tech starts producing immediately.

items.name: Lock in a recurring calendar
items.text: A signed annual or semi-annual schedule lets the vendor plan routes and usually earns 5% to 15% off one-time pricing.

blocks.text: Chemistry and equipment expectations at both sizes

The process should not get cheaper by cutting corners. Whether the order is 12 chairs or 180, expect HEPA pre-vacuuming, a fabric-appropriate pre-spray, documented dwell time, and heated extraction with good recovery. Green-certified offices often specify plant-derived, low-VOC chemistry; a product such as ECOS Pro Orange Plus all-purpose cleaner, an EPA Safer Choice, plant-based, low-VOC 1-gallon concentrate, is the sort of neutral cleaner vendors use for pre-cleaning hard chair bases, arms, and panel trim before extraction. On large floors, vendors frequently schedule hard-floor work in the same nights. A 13-inch random-orbit machine like the Bissell Commercial BGEM9000 suits small suites and tight aisles, while a 17-inch, 175 RPM, 1.5 HP rotary such as the Powr-Flite M171-3 covers VCT corridors on bigger floors faster. Bundling floor care and upholstery into one mobilization is another way to unlock volume pricing.

blocks.title: Ask for unit prices at two volumes
blocks.text: Request a quote at your actual quantity and at 1.5 times that quantity. The difference shows how much of the price is fixed setup, which tells you whether bundling extra seating or a second floor is worth it.

faqs.q: Why does my small office pay more per chair than a large company?
faqs.a: Vendors carry fixed setup, travel, and minimum charges of roughly $90–$135 per visit or $175–$250 per project. On a 12-chair order that overhead adds several dollars per chair; on a 140-chair order it is negligible. Production is also faster with two-person crews on large floors.

faqs.q: At what size do vendors usually waive minimum charges?
faqs.a: Most vendors waive minimums or mobilization fees once a single order exceeds about $750–$1,000, which typically corresponds to 40 or more workstations, or a smaller office that bundles chairs, panels, and carpet spotting.

faqs.q: Do large buildings need different safety documentation?
faqs.a: The requirements are the same, but larger jobs involve more crew members, so verify each tech has OSHA HazCom training and access to Safety Data Sheets, that bloodborne pathogen procedures exist for any biological stains, and that the vendor's certificate of insurance meets landlord limits for multi-night work.

faqs.q: How should I compare a per-hour quote with a per-chair quote?
faqs.a: Divide the hourly rate by the vendor's stated production rate. At $55–$95 per hour and 4 to 7 chairs per hour, the implied per-chair price is about $8–$24. If one vendor quotes hourly and another per chair, convert both to per workstation using the same scope.

faqs.q: Is it worth splitting a large floor into phases?
faqs.a: Phasing by department across several nights is often necessary for dry time and electrical capacity. Ask the vendor to price the full floor as one contract with phased execution so you keep the volume discount instead of being billed as several small jobs.
